client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. It's like the color has drained out of everything — things I used to enjoy just feel flat and pointless now. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because nothing is really going to bring him back, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy — that quiet, grey kind of grief where even the things you love lose their light. You're right that nothing will bring him back, and I don't want to pretend otherwise; but sometimes talking isn't about fixing the loss, it's about making a little more room to breathe inside it. What was he like — what do you miss most about him?

client: His name was Biscuit, and he was this goofy, scruffy terrier mix who always seemed to know when I was having a bad day. He'd just come and sit right on my feet, like he was anchoring me to the ground. I miss that the most, I think — that feeling of not being alone in a room, because he was always just... there.
therapist: Biscuit sounds like he was truly special — that quiet, steady presence he offered you, just anchoring you without needing anything to be said, is such a profound kind of love. It makes complete sense that what you're grieving isn't just him, but also that feeling of being held and not alone. When you notice that emptiness now — that space where he used to be — what tends to go through your mind in those moments?

client: Mostly I just feel this wave of guilt, honestly. Like I keep replaying the last few weeks and wondering if I should have taken him to the vet sooner, or if he was in pain and I just didn't notice. It's like my brain won't let me just miss him — it has to make it my fault somehow.
therapist: That guilt your mind keeps reaching for — it sounds exhausting, like grief isn't allowed to just be grief without your brain turning it into a trial. This is something we see a lot in CBT: when we're in pain, our minds sometimes try to create a sense of control by finding fault, because "I should have done something" feels more bearable than "there was nothing I could have done." Can you tell me — if a close friend described making the same choices you made with Biscuit, would you hold them as responsible as you're holding yourself?

client: I know what you're getting at, and logically I can see it — I would never blame a friend the way I'm blaming myself. But when I try to apply that same thinking to myself, it just doesn't land the same way, it feels almost like I'd be letting myself off the hook too easily. Like the guilt is the only thing I have left that proves how much he mattered to me.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — that the guilt feels like proof of love, like releasing it would somehow mean Biscuit mattered less. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: the grief itself, the colour draining from the world, the way you still light up describing his scruffy face and the weight of him on your feet — that *is* the proof of how much he mattered. What do you think it might feel like to let the love be the evidence, instead of the guilt?

client: Honestly, that idea feels both really beautiful and kind of terrifying at the same time. Like, the guilt is uncomfortable but it's also familiar — it's something I know how to do, whereas just sitting with the love and the loss without the self-blame feels almost too open, too vulnerable. I'm not sure I know how to do that without it feeling like I'm just... floating with no anchor.
therapist: That image of floating without an anchor is so telling — especially from someone whose greatest comfort was *being* anchored, by Biscuit sitting right on your feet. It makes complete sense that vulnerability feels disorienting when the thing that used to ground you is gone. I wonder if, rather than letting go of the anchor all at once, we could think about building a new relationship with the love and the loss gradually — in small, manageable moments. What's one small way you already honour how much Biscuit meant to you, outside of the guilt?

client: There's this photo of him on my phone that I look at sometimes — not in a sad, punishing way, but just because it makes me smile for a second before the ache comes back. I guess that's something, even if it feels small and almost accidental rather than intentional. I never really thought of that as honoring him, it just kind of happens.
therapist: That moment with the photo — that little flicker of a smile — is actually really significant, and I love that you noticed it. It's not accidental at all; some part of you is already reaching toward the love rather than the guilt, even without trying. What might it feel like to make that one small moment a little more intentional — to let yourself look at that photo and just sit with the smile, even for a few seconds before the ache arrives?

client: I think I could maybe try that, but I'm a little worried that intentionally sitting with it will somehow make the ache hit harder than when it just happens naturally. Like right now it's this brief accidental thing, and I'm scared that if I slow down and really lean into it, I'll just end up crying and feeling worse. Does that make sense, or am I just finding reasons to avoid it?
therapist: It makes complete sense, and I want to say — the fact that you're asking "am I avoiding it?" shows a lot of self-awareness. You're right that leaning in might bring tears, and that's not nothing; but in CBT we'd gently distinguish between pain that overwhelms and pain that moves through you, and a few intentional seconds with Biscuit's photo is unlikely to break you open in the way your mind is predicting. What if the goal wasn't to avoid the ache, but just to see if the smile and the ache can exist together, even briefly?

client: That framing actually helps a little — thinking of it as the smile and the ache coexisting rather than one defeating the other. I guess I've been treating them like they can't both be true at the same time, like if I feel the love fully then the grief will swallow me whole. Maybe I could try it once this week and just see what happens, though I'm not making any promises about how it'll go.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in what you just said — that love and grief can coexist, that one doesn't have to defeat the other. That's actually a quiet but important shift in how you're seeing this, and you arrived at it yourself. No promises needed — just try it once, and whatever happens, we can talk about it; you don't have to face what comes up alone.

client: That last part — "you don't have to face what comes up alone" — actually hit me harder than I expected, because I think that's been part of what makes this so hard. Biscuit was who I turned to when things felt heavy, and now that he's gone, I don't really have that in my life anymore. I'm not sure one photo moment is going to fix that bigger loneliness underneath everything.
therapist: You've just named something really important that goes deeper than grief for Biscuit — a loneliness that he was quietly holding at bay, and that his absence has now made impossible to ignore. That's not a small thing, and you're right that one photo moment won't touch it; but I'm glad it's surfacing here, because it deserves attention in its own right. Can you tell me a little more about what connection looks like in your life right now — are there people around, even if it doesn't feel like quite the same kind of safe?

client: There are people around — a couple of friends, my sister — but it's not the same, because with people there's always this layer of performance, like I have to be okay enough not to worry them. Biscuit never needed me to be okay, he just accepted whatever state I was in. I do talk to my sister sometimes but I always end up downplaying how bad it actually feels because I don't want to be a burden.
therapist: What you had with Biscuit — that completely unconditional, no-performance-required acceptance — is actually quite rare, and it makes sense that human connection feels more effortful by comparison. But I notice something worth gently exploring: the story that you'd be "a burden" to your sister is a thought, not a fact, and it's quietly keeping you isolated in the very moment you most need to be held. What do you imagine your sister would actually say if she knew how much you'd been downplaying things?
